clue.text: Bowled over by sale price goods, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to be bowled over is to be floored, sent sprawling
goods sold off at a reduced price, or under the auctioneer's hammer, are described this way

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrase: flattened in a fall, and reduced in price or sold at auction.

clue.text: Pre-eminent person with a prize flower

parts.note: the top figure in any field is its king
a cup is a trophy awarded as a prize

explanation.surface: A leading figure picks up a trophy for a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A marsh marigold, a yellow wild bloom of wet meadows, goes by this name.

clue.text: Nothing unusual about a deck hand

definitions.text: Nothing unusual about a deck hand

parts.words: Nothing unusual about a deck hand
parts.note: the clue reads as a remark that a sailor is unremarkable, and the naval rank for the lowest grade of sailor is made of a word for unremarkable plus a word for sailor

explanation.surface: A comment that a sailor working on deck is quite unremarkable.
explanation.definitionFit: The most junior rating in the Royal Navy is the deck hand of the lowest grade.

clue.text: Give a touch of lip-service

parts.note: lip-service usually means empty words, but here it is a service done with the lips, a touch of them

explanation.surface: Someone offers token, insincere agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing one's lips to someone is literally a service performed with the lips.

clue.text: To the physician anything but an ill wind

definitions.text: To the physician anything but an ill wind

parts.words: To the physician anything but an ill wind
parts.note: one word means both a current of cold air, the ill wind, and a dose of medicine, which a doctor sees as wholly good

explanation.surface: A doctor reckons a certain breeze does nobody harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's an ill wind that blows nobody any good' is a proverb; the doctor's sense of the word is a medicinal potion, not a breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: A dose of liquid medicine is called this, as is a cold current of air indoors.

clue.text: See 1
Adornment last month over a sovereign

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece written over another comes first

parts.note: December is the final month of the year, shortened to DEC
a king is a sovereign ruler

explanation.surface: A monarch's finery is put on display at the end of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: Decoration such as flags and bunting hung up for a festivity is called by this name.

clue.text: A real blow to West Ham United

parts.note: W is the compass abbreviation for west
taken as written from the club's name

explanation.surface: A football supporter laments a heavy defeat for West Ham United, the London club.
explanation.walkthrough: West Ham United is a London football club; 'United' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A forceful thump or hit is expressed by this exclamation word.

clue.text: City of 10 holding ship's record

indicators.note: the answer to 10 holds the record inside it, around the middle

parts.note: the answer to clue 10, a traffic marker
a log is the official record of a ship's voyage

explanation.surface: A city linked to another clue keeps a vessel's records.
explanation.definitionFit: A large German city on the Rhine, famous for its cathedral and scented water.

clue.text: Did she bestow her favours impartially on both sides of the Medway?

definitions.text: Did she bestow her favours impartially on both sides of the Medway?

parts.words: Did she bestow her favours impartially on both sides of the Medway?
parts.note: the Medway divides Kent into Men of Kent and Kentish Men, so an impartial, or fair, young woman of that county is pictured

explanation.surface: A question about a young woman's even-handed romances along a Kent river.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is an English county; tradition says those born east of the river Medway are Men of Kent and those west of it Kentish Men. 'Fair' means even-handed as well as lovely.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional name for a Kentish girl, also a variety of cherry and an old song title.

clue.text: Very near to being friendly?

definitions.meaning: describes two places right beside each other
someone who is not distant at all is warm and friendly

explanation.definitionFit: Spatial closeness, and the opposite of aloofness, since an unfriendly person is called distant.

clue.text: Once placed with others guarding a no-go area

definitions.text: with others guarding a no-go area

indicators.note: the letters of the word are set down, placed in a new order

explanation.surface: A one-time arrangement with colleagues protecting a forbidden zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed' rearranges ONCE; the definition pictures road markers set out in a row around a closed-off area.
explanation.definitionFit: A traffic marker is set out in a line with its fellows to close off a stretch of road.

clue.text: Another turnover at the polls?

parts.note: read as two words it is a seat captured by one party from another in an election, while as one word it means once more

explanation.surface: Asking if voters will change their allegiance at a further election.
explanation.definitionFit: Once more, another time; split into two words it is an election victory taken from a rival.

clue.text: It's back on the march for this creature

definitions.text: It's back on the march for this creature

parts.words: It's back on the march for this creature
parts.note: in the punishment named after this amphibian, a captive is carried along by four people face down, back uppermost

explanation.surface: Something returning to the parade for an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'frog-march' carried a prisoner face down, so the back is the uppermost part on that march.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailless leaping amphibian gives its name to a way of hauling a prisoner along.

clue.text: Game fellow

definitions.meaning: any athletic pastime or competitive activity
an old-fashioned friendly term for a decent chap, as in 'old boy'

explanation.definitionFit: An athletic pastime, and a good-natured chap as in 'be a good one'.

clue.text: Impressive stamps

parts.note: impressive here means making an impression in wax, so the stamps are devices that press a design

explanation.surface: Postage stamps that are striking to look at.
explanation.definitionFit: Engraved devices pressed into wax to authenticate a document, so they literally make impressions.

clue.text: Mimic in role is on edge

indicators.note: the mimic sits inside the word for a role

parts.note: an actor's part is a role
to ape is to mimic

explanation.surface: An impressionist playing a part feels nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: A low protective wall running along the outer rim of a roof or bridge.

clue.text: Angered about something delivered by hand

indicators.note: the letters of the word are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone furious about a parcel that came by courier.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bomb thrown by hand is the item delivered here.

clue.text: Place of high standing, so to speak

definitions.text: Place of high standing, so to speak

parts.words: Place of high standing, so to speak
parts.note: a raised spot where one stands high in order to speak, not a place of high rank

explanation.surface: A position of prestige, figuratively speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised platform for a public speaker, so the person stands high to speak.

clue.text: The following train

definitions.meaning: a body of followers or attendants
a train is a group of attendants trailing a dignitary

explanation.definitionFit: A group of attendants accompanying an important person; both clue words name such an entourage.

clue.text: Got by but the responsibility left its mark

definitions.meaning: to get by is to cope or survive
split as two words it says the fellow grew older under the strain, a man who aged

explanation.definitionFit: Coped or survived; split in two, a fellow who grew old from the burden.

clue.text: Proctor's prowler at Oxbridge

parts.note: at Oxford and Cambridge the proctor, a disciplinary official, was escorted on patrol by attendants nicknamed after a fierce breed of dog

explanation.surface: A university official's lurking hound.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxbridge means Oxford and Cambridge universities, whose proctors keep student discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname for a proctor's attendant at the old universities, borrowed from a stocky British dog breed.

clue.text: All shipshape and fashion

parts.note: the clue quotes the old naval saying meaning everything in good order, with the name of a port missing before its last word

explanation.surface: Everything neat and stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shipshape and Bristol fashion' is a British phrase meaning orderly; the missing word is the port city in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The English port city completes the seafaring phrase for perfect tidiness.

clue.text: They're sightseeing girls at Gateshead

indicators.note: the head letter of the town is placed at the front of the next piece

parts.note: lasses are girls, especially in the north of England

explanation.surface: Young women from Gateshead out on a tour.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England, where 'lasses' is the usual word for girls; its head letter G is added at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles help the wearer see, so they are a sight aid.

clue.text: Late out for a duck

indicators.note: the letters are put out of their order

explanation.surface: A bird that slips away after hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A small freshwater dabbling bird of the wildfowl family.

clue.text: Not prepared for fun exercise it follows

indicators.note: the second word comes after the rearranged first
the letters are worked or exercised into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone out of condition after a bit of light-hearted physical training.
explanation.definitionFit: Unready or unsuitable for a task or for fighting.

clue.text: No longer devoted to a King of Mercia

parts.note: to have gone off someone is to have lost your liking for them

explanation.surface: A subject has lost loyalty to an Anglo-Saxon monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom of central England; its eighth-century ruler built the famous dyke along the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighth-century ruler of Mercia, builder of the great earthwork dyke.

clue.text: Wine for a good man in first-class condition

indicators.note: the good man sits inside the first-class term

parts.note: A1 means first-rate condition, written with the letter I for the figure one
ST, saint, is a holy or good man

explanation.surface: A drink for a decent fellow in fine shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkling white from Piedmont in northern Italy.

clue.text: Keenness gives an advantage

definitions.meaning: a sharpness, as on a blade or in a voice
a slight lead over a rival, as in having the upper hand

explanation.definitionFit: Sharpness of a blade or tone, and a slight lead over rivals.

clue.text: See 9 with this incapacity

parts.note: clue 9 means very close, so someone with this eye defect can see only what is close by

explanation.surface: A cross-reference instruction with a disability attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See 9' looks like a cross-reference, but 'See' is the verb: the sufferer sees only things at no distance at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Myopia, the eye condition in which only close objects are seen clearly.

clue.text: Charitable strain

explanation.definitionFit: Generous in nature, and a type or breed, as in 'of that sort'.

clue.text: Foiled by Hamlet he suffered a real setback

indicators.note: the two words suffer and are knocked into a new order

parts.note: fodder, taken as written
read as two words, set back gives the letters of set turned backwards

explanation.surface: A man beaten in a sword fight by Hamlet had a serious reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffered' rearranges REAL into LAER; 'setback' is read as 'set' back, TES. In Shakespeare's play Hamlet kills this man in a fencing match.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia's brother, who duels with the prince in the final scene of the Shakespeare tragedy.
